item.title: China urges Japan's leaders to heed voices of justice at home: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 18:33:00
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning In response to former Japanese foreign minister and Chair of the Association for the Promotion of International Trade Takeshi Iwaya's remarks following his visit to China that Japan was responsible for the deterioration in China-Japan relations and that the Japanese government should seek ways to improve ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the remarks reflected the rationality and conscience of insightful people in Japan and were positively viewed by China. When asked to comment on the voices in Japan that criticize the evasion of historical responsibility for leading Japan’s China policy astray and call on the Japanese government to face up to and address the problem, Mao said during a press briefing on Monday that as they pointed out, the root cause and essence of the problem lie in the serious distortions and errors in the Japanese leadership’s view of history and of China, which have severely undermined the political foundation of China-Japan relations. Mao said that this situation serves the interests of neither side, and Japan bears full responsibility for it, adding that the onus was on Japan to put bilateral ties back on track. We urge Japan’s current leaders to listen to and heed voices of justice at home, face up to the root causes of the problems, abide by the four political documents between China and Japan, and genuinely reflect on and correct their mistakes on issues concerning Taiwan island, history and their understanding of China, Mao added. Global Times

item.title: China issues guideline to strengthen crackdown on food safety crimes
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 17:25:00
Staff members from the Xiajiang County Administration for Market Regulation conduct tests on vegetables sold at a supermarket in Xiajiang county, East China's Jiangxi Province, on September 22, 2026. Photo: VCG China's top political and legal affairs authority has issued a guideline calling for stronger efforts to investigate and punish food safety violations and crimes, with particular attention to meat products, food served in schools, health food products, vegetables and fruit. The guideline also calls for strict adherence to the "four strictest" requirements to ensure food safety, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Monday. The guideline also calls for stricter handling of cases throughout criminal proceedings, including tighter restrictions on the use of suspended sentences and exemptions from criminal punishment. Offenders involved in serious cases with severe social impact should face heavier penalties in accordance with the law. The document was issued as food safety offenses increasingly involve networks, specialized operations and organized activity spanning longer supply chains, while gaps remain in coordination between administrative law enforcement and criminal justice, an official with the Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the CPC Central Committee said in an explanation of the guideline on Monday. The official also pointed to a series of recent criminal incidents, including "formaldehyde-treated cabbage," the use of the pesticide dichlorvos for disinfection, and bayberries soaked in chemical solutions, saying such cases had seriously compromised food safety and drawn widespread public concern. The official noted that China's food safety work should continue to follow the "four strictest" requirements, namely the strictest standards, the strictest supervision, the strictest punishment and the strictest accountability, to safeguard public health and ensure food safety. Under the guideline, enforcement will focus not only on particular types of food but also on key parts of the supply chain, including production and processing, online sales, catering services and food imports. Authorities are also required to strengthen supervision and guidance over major, difficult and complex food safety cases. The guideline says criminal penalties should be used to substantially raise the cost of violations and deter businesses from breaking the law. Another focus is specific measures to close gaps between administrative enforcement and criminal proceedings. The guideline calls for clearer standards on when cases should be transferred for criminal investigation, as well as rules covering testing and appraisal and the conversion of evidence collected in administrative cases for use in criminal proceedings. Authorities are also asked to address practices such as substituting administrative fines for criminal prosecution or failing to impose administrative penalties where warranted. An information-sharing platform is to be established to improve coordination, while mechanisms for transferring cases back from the criminal justice system for administrative handling will also be improved. The guideline also calls for accelerating a comprehensive revision of China's Food Safety Law to address the rapid growth of new forms of online businesses. Regulatory requirements are expected to be further clarified for fresh food e-commerce, food delivery services and livestreaming e-commerce, with responsibilities assigned more clearly to the parties involved. The guideline also calls for a legal liability system in which penalties are proportionate to the seriousness of violations and set at different levels. Authorities will also work to standardize the application of law in food safety cases through measures including the publication of typical cases and the inclusion of relevant cases in the People's Courts Case Database. For newly detected illegal additives, the guideline calls for relevant departments to update the list of prohibited substances in a timely manner so that new forms of food safety crime can be dealt with under clearer legal and policy standards. To prevent food safety problems at their source, judicial, procuratorial and public security authorities are urged to issue judicial recommendations, procuratorial recommendations and police alerts when investigations expose broader risks or regulatory loopholes in the food supply chain. The guideline also calls for greater use of big-data legal supervision models and public-interest litigation to help regulators identify leads, rectify problems in relevant industries and shift food safety governance toward earlier prevention. The Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the CPC Central Committee will coordinate implementation, while the Supreme People's Court, the Supreme People's Procuratorate, the Ministry of Public Security and the Ministry of Justice will work together and make specific arrangements within their respective systems to carry out the guideline, according to Xinhua. item.title: Certain politicians serve as pawns of Taiwan authorities seeking 'independence' by relying on external forces: FM spokesperson on countermeasures against Paraguayan and Belizean ministers
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 16:14:00
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs The Taiwan question is a major issue of principle concerning China's sovereignty and national reunification, representing the core of China's core interests, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing on Monday, following China's countermeasures against Paraguayan and Belizean ministers over their "egregious remarks and actions" regarding the Taiwan question. Certain politicians from Paraguay and Belize have acted as pawns for the Taiwan authorities, which seek "independence" by relying on external forces, said Mao. They made illicit visits to Taiwan and received Taiwan separatist figures, gravely interfering in China's internal affairs. They spread disinformation about alleged Chinese cyberattacks and smeared China, creating grave adverse international repercussions, the spokesperson said. In response to such misconduct, China has issued a Foreign Ministry order announcing countermeasures in accordance with the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law of the People's Republic of China, to impose penalties on the individuals concerned and deter others from following suit, the spokesperson added. According to Chinese Foreign Ministry's announcement earlier on Monday, Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego, Paraguay's minister of information and communication technologies, and Francis Fonseca, Belize's minister for foreign affairs, foreign trade, education, culture, science and technology, are denied visas or entry into China, including its Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions, according to the ministry. All organizations and individuals within China shall be prohibited from engaging in transaction, cooperation and other activities with them, the ministry added. Global Times

item.title: Led by DeepSeek, Chinese AI models take top five positions in global weekly token usage ranking
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 15:42:00
AI photo: VCG Chinese AI models have taken the top five spots in weekly token usage, according to the latest data from OpenRouter, a global large language model (LLM) aggregation platform. From October 5 to 11, AI models worldwide processed 172 trillion tokens, up 3.61 percent week over week. Chinese models accounted for 86.74 trillion tokens, compared with 18.97 trillion for US AI models. Token usage by Chinese AI models grew by 50.96 percent week over week, while usage by US models increased by 17.1 percent, the National Business Daily reported on Monday. This marked the 24th consecutive week that Chinese models led their US counterparts in token usage. A token is the basic unit of text processed by an AI model and it has become a key measure of AI usage and computing consumption. Chinese AI venture DeepSeek, which shook the tech industry last year by challenging US assumptions about China's AI capabilities, led the ranking. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash processed 41 trillion tokens during the week, up 60 percent week over week. The other AI models in the top five also came from Chinese companies. Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash ranked second, processing 12.2 trillion tokens during the week, up 26 percent week-over-week. Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Flash came in third, processing 11.5 trillion tokens, up 19 percent week-over-week. Shanghai-based AI firm StepFun's Step 5 Preview ranked fourth, processing 8.84 trillion tokens. Tencent Hy4 preview ranked fifth, processing 8.28 trillion tokens, up 27 percent week over week. It was not the first time that Chinese AI models had taken all five top spots in the ranking. Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 ranked eighth, processing 5.02 trillion tokens, up 104 percent week over week. During the week, the five leading Chinese models accounted for 47.9 percent of tokens processed. Chinese analysts said the models' strong weekly performance underscored rapid growth in global uses as developers worldwide increasingly turned to Chinese companies' low-cost, open-weight models. Tian Feng, president of the Fast Think Institute and former dean of the Intelligence Industry Research Institute at SenseTime, told the Global Times that the ranking represented an overall endorsement of Chinese models' capabilities, stability and cost-effectiveness. DeepSeek's performance was particularly noteworthy because the company significantly raised API prices for its latest flagship models in mid-August. "The weekly data again demonstrated that overseas enterprises and developers are treating Chinese models as serious options and evaluated them carefully when choosing LLMs," Tian said. Global corporate adoption of Chinese models increased substantially in 2026, according to CNBC. Chinese models accounted for just 6-13 percent of uses on OpenRouter in February.

item.title: Long March Origin choir carries forward Red Army spirit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 11:44:00
Zou Weimin (1st L), the director of the Long March Origin choir, conducts a performance at a middle school in Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, Sept. 3, 2026. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. As one of its important starting points, Yudu County in east China's Jiangxi Province, a place best known as the starting point of the Long March by the Central Red Army, the historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history, has become more than a place of remembrance. It was from Yudu that more than 80,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the Yudu River and began the Long March in 1934, the roughly 12,500-kilometer trek later described by American journalist Harrison Salisbury as "a great human epic." On the stone tablet in front of the memorial museum of the Central Red Army's departure for the Long March here in Yudu, three Chinese characters meaning "Long March Origin" are engraved. The "Long March Origin" not only indicates that this place was the starting point of the important strategic transfer of the Red Army at that time, but also carries the profound understanding of the Long March spirit by the people of Yudu to this day. You can see the words "Long March Origin" frequently in Yudu, and the Long March Origin choir is a prominent presence. In this red revolutionary land of Yudu, almost everyone can share family stories connected to the Red Army's Long March. The Long March Origin choir, established in 2010, is composed of over 100 descendants of Red Army soldiers from all walks of life in the county. Over these years, they have not only performed the "Suite of Songs on the Long March" in Yudu and across Jiangxi in their spare time, but also carried forward the spirit of the Long March along the Long March route with their songs. The choir's first performance was staged on June 30, 2011, which was dedicated to the 90th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China. So far the choir has performed over 730 charity performances. "We hope that the choir will complete 1,000 performances by the 100th anniversary of the victory of the Long March," said Zou Weimin, the director of the choir. item.title: Botswana aims to strengthen, deepen ties with China, says Botswanan president
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 09:18:00
Botswanan President Duma Gideon Boko speaks at an exclusive interview with Xinhua in Gaborone, Botswana, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Wei) The Botswana-China relationship is "deep and strong," and Botswana looks forward to deepening bilateral cooperation in trade, the digital economy, renewable energy and other fields, Botswanan President Duma Gideon Boko has said. In an interview with Xinhua ahead of his first state visit to China since taking office, Boko said that the two sides have maintained "very good, very strong, (and) mutually beneficial diplomatic relationship" for many years. "China has, over those years, provided immense development assistance to the Republic of Botswana," he said, noting that Botswana looks forward to benefiting from Chinese expertise, including that of companies already operating in Botswana. "We look forward to broadening and deepening that presence, and inviting others that will participate in mega projects in Botswana," he said. Botswana is also looking to deepen the trade relationship with China in other ways, including partnering with Chinese companies which "have done massive investment in research and development in relation to beneficiation," Boko said, adding that it would "enable Botswana to become a manufacturer and, therefore, serve the Chinese market even better." From May 1 this year, China extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties. Regarding the measure as "a very welcome and laudable step by the Chinese government," Boko said that it has opened up "what is a 1.4 billion market in terms of consumer base to African products." "It makes the trade relations between Africa and China seamless, and will help our economies," he said. "But more importantly, with regard to Botswana, we will be concluding agreements that will enable our citrus produce to enter China under the no-tariff arrangement, which is massive as a benefit to our country." On digitalization and economic diversification, Boko said that Botswana looks forward to benefiting from the Chinese expertise. "China has the ability, the strength, and the capability ... to deploy those capabilities in Botswana for the benefit of the economy of Botswana, and the broader economy of the SADC (Southern African Development Community) region and the African continent," he said. The Botswanan president also said that China's development experience in renewable energy, energy storage, power infrastructure and other green industries is exactly what Botswana needs, adding that his country is open to Chinese businesses. "We are looking forward to meeting those companies, (and) giving them facts about the country and the opportunities, so that they can then choose to deploy their expertise and technologies in the country," he said. "We certainly look forward to working with China in these regards, and it basically is a matter of building upon a foundation, a very firm and strong foundation that already exists," he added.

item.title: Journey of a single pickup truck shows the value transition of 'In China, for the world': Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 23:57:00
Visitors gather at the 29th Chengdu International Auto Show held at the Western China International Expo City in Chengdu, Southwest China's Sichuan Province, on August 21, 2026. The 10-day fair covers an exhibition area of 220,000 square meters and brought together nearly 120 major domestic and international automobile brands, with about 1,600 vehicles on display. Photo: VCG The cross-border journey of a single pickup truck breaks the long-standing inertia of technology flowing "from West to East" and mirrors the profound reshaping of the global economic landscape. Today, "In China, for the world" has evolved into its version 2.0, with more products and technologies defined, developed, and manufactured in China serving global markets and helping foreign automakers catch the new wave of opportunities. It was reported that the Frontier Pro, the first model of Nissan designed, developed and manufactured in China for global export, will officially hit the Mexican market this month. It will later be rolled out progressively across Latin America, the Middle East, Australia and other markets. While the Frontier Pro is merely one specific example within the global industrial landscape, it reflects a plain truth: China today is no longer just an assembly line and sales market for multinationals, but also a source of global innovation and a joint creator of value. The phrase "In China, for the World" carries deeper and broader implications amid the high-quality development of China's economy. Nissan is not an isolated case in the global auto industry. Partnering with China's supply chain to go global amounts to securing a reliable "ticket for the voyage" - a consensus shared by a growing number of foreign automakers. SAIC-GM has extended its joint venture term by 20 years, with the Buick Electra E7 being shipped overseas from China. SAIC Volkswagen renewed its contract six years ahead of schedule and exports multiple vehicle models to Uzbekistan. Changan Mazda leverages its Nanjing plant to ship overseas variants of the EZ-6 to more than 20 countries and regions. China FAW Group, Toyota Motor Corporation and GAC Group, long-standing partners, have signed a new strategic cooperation framework agreement in Guangzhou. If "manufacturing capability" was one of the draws for foreign enterprises to set up roots in China, then China's "smart manufacturing capacity" gives their industrial upgrading and global footprint an extra boost. In the past, the mantra of "In China, for China" among major auto giants represented "exchanging technology for market access." The "In China, for the world" version 1.0 simply meant "Made in China, exported to the world." Today, however, "In China, for the world" has evolved into its version 2.0, with more products and technologies defined, developed, and manufactured in China serving global markets and helping foreign automakers catch the new wave of opportunities. This evolution means that the Chinese market has become an "innovation incubator" and "transformation accelerator," with China-foreign automotive cooperation entering a new phase where China's industrial chain feeds back into the global market. Innovation under the "In China, for the world" framework is not merely about multinationals ramping up investment to tap into China's innovation capability. More importantly, it fosters an "innovation ecosystem" in China where Chinese and foreign firms grow side by side. China boasts the world's largest new-energy vehicle market, the most complete industrial chain and the largest workforce of R&D personnel. Chinese manufacturing is shifting from "product export" to "technology export," and from "shipping goods overseas" to "exporting industrial ecosystems." It has achieved a historic leap from the one-way cycle of "China supplies, the world consumes" to two-way empowerment through "technology collaboration and ecosystem co-creation." The old one-way model of "market for technology" has been upgraded into a two-way partnership, with Chinese and foreign sides acting as mutual "technology partners." Modern joint ventures are no longer a simple grafting of production capacity, but instead represent deep integration between accumulated global technological expertise and China's innovative dynamism. According to statistics released by financial services firm UBS, since 2018, European automakers including Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz Group and BMW Group have established technology partnerships with at least 38 Chinese companies and research institutions, covering areas such as software, hardware, batteries, and vehicle connectivity. Nissan has designated China as its global hub for innovation and exports. Volkswagen has built a full design-build-test-validate cycle in Hefei, dubbed "China's Wolfsburg." Renault, Porsche, Kia and others have all made choices aligned with this trend. Multinational automakers are unanimously repositioning China from a "sales destination" to an "R&D cradle" and "global export hub." This is a vote of confidence backed by real capital, and a clear verdict delivered by industrial logic. Facts have proven that China's new-energy industry never creates a zero-sum game where one side gains at the expense of the other; instead, it offers long-term opportunities for shared growth. The latest figures show that Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory delivered more than 95,000 vehicles in September, hitting its highest monthly output this year. In the six and a half years since it went into operation, the Shanghai Gigafactory has produced over 4.5 million electric vehicles, accounting for more than 45 percent of Tesla's global output. China's vast market remains an opportunity for the world. Meanwhile, "international collaboration" and "technological innovation," as fast-growing components of China's development dividends, are being shared by more countries and enterprises across the globe. The automotive industry epitomizes economic globalization. The cross-border journey of a single pickup truck carries jobs, innovation and future prospects across industrial chains. It breaks the long-standing inertia of technology flowing "from West to East" and mirrors the profound reshaping of the global economic landscape. This new path of "In China, for the world" leads toward a greener, more efficient and inclusive tomorrow. If the world thrives, China will thrive, and if China thrives, the world will be even better. Noises that seek to swim against the tide and erect barriers will ultimately be repelled by irrefutable facts.

item.title: How Belt and Road rail links redefine globalization for landlocked nations
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 23:00:00
The China-Laos Railway has completed four years of safe operations, carrying more than 62.5 million passenger trips and 72.5 million tons of cargo as of December 2, 2025. Photo: courtesy of China State Railway Group As of October 9, cumulative trade on the China-Laos Railway has passed 100 billion yuan (about $14.9 billion), with more than 20.77 million tons of import and export goods moved. In the first eight months of 2026, rail imports of Southeast Asian tropical fruits totaled 5.26 billion yuan, while exports of machinery and electrical products during the same period reached 7.42 billion yuan, up 58.4 percent year-on-year. Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia. With no coastline, all imports and exports must pass through neighboring ports and roads. That means higher freight costs, longer delays and more spoilage. The UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) estimates that landlocked developing countries face trade costs roughly 50 percent higher than their coastal peers. Of the 32 landlocked developing countries worldwide, 17 are also classified as least developed. Globalization over the past few decades has largely been driven by maritime trade. A landlocked country is inherently marginalized within that network. It is not that these countries fail to try; rather, the network was never designed to connect them. Laos used to be in exactly this position. Its goods had to leave through Thai or Vietnamese ports, leaving it with little say over price or timing. A farmer could expect to lose a fifth of his produce due to spoilage on the way to the port. A businessman importing equipment had to wait for a neighbor to clear customs. Geography had locked the country in, and the UN Development Programme has long listed Laos among the least developed countries. The railway changed that. The 1,035-kilometer line opened in December 2021. The fastest trains now run from Vientiane to Kunming in 9 hours and 36 minutes. The railway turned Laos from a country the network had forgotten about into a key node within it. It would be too simple to describe this as "China built Laos a railway." Laos has plugged into a new network whose nodes include Kunming, Vientiane, Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, and which may one day reach Singapore. In this network, Laos has moved from the periphery to a hub. The figure of 100 billion yuan is not the most important part. What matters is the change in development logic behind it. In the past, a landlocked country had one route into global trade: borrowing a neighbor's port to reach the sea. It depended on that neighbor's ports, roads and customs, and every checkpoint added cost and uncertainty. Now railways, pipelines, digital networks and regional power grids are changing the fate of landlocked states. UNCTAD noted that landlocked developing countries have long accounted for less than 1 percent of global trade. However, that figure is starting to change, and the China-Laos Railway is one example. In Africa, the Addis Ababa-Djibouti Railway links landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti's port. In Central Asia, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway is still in the planning stages. These lines share one commonality: They are not simply opening a path to the sea; they are creating nodes, and those nodes provide many young people with opportunities they have never had. When Western media discuss the Belt and Road Initiative, they often ask whether it is a "debt trap." We believe that question points in the wrong direction. The real question is not who owes whom, but who has been connected. Laos has been connected. It has gone from "land-locked" to "land-linked." A trip from Vientiane to Kunming that once took days now takes under 10 hours. Durian spoilage has fallen from about 20 percent to approximately 5 percent. Young people who were once reluctant to work in factories now want to learn technical skills. When the road opens, goods move, people travel and technology spreads. Extensions of the line are already under construction, from Vientiane to Thailand and from Vientiane to Vung Ang port in Vietnam. Once these extensions are complete, Laos will be more than just land-linked. What matters even more is the direction of travel, both north and south. Durians go north, and electric vehicles go south, with people moving back and forth in between. The logic of globalization is shifting from being sea-driven to a combination of land and sea. For landlocked countries, this represents their first real opportunity.

item.title: GT Voice: China's rapid progress in robotics offers South Korea opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 21:08:00
Illustration: Liu Xidan/GT The economic potential of humanoid robots extends beyond the machines themselves. The Chosun Daily reported on Sunday, citing Counterpoint Research, that demand for DRAM chips used in the "brains" of humanoid robots equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to grow more than 20-fold by 2030. The projected growth has raised hopes that humanoid robots could become a new source of growth for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, top DRAM memory chipmakers in the world. As humanoid robotics quickly develops and progresses, China has established a substantial presence in this field. Chinese media outlets have reported that more than 140 Chinese companies were researching and developing humanoid robots in 2025, while a widely cited market study estimated that robots made in China accounted for 84.7 percent of global shipments last year. The growth of China's robotics sector creates massive opportunities for South Korean DRAM suppliers. Yet normal market competition with Chinese enterprises appears to be a concern in South Korea. In a separate article, The Chosun Daily reported that during the audit done by the country's National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee on October 6, criticism was voiced that South Korea's investment in humanoid robotics lagged behind China's. And, two humanoid robots made by Chinese companies were brought to the audit to illustrate the gap between the two countries. The robots walked into the meeting room, shook hands with a representative and performed a dance. The demonstration offered a glimpse of South Korea's concerns about the gap in robotics development with China. China's advances in humanoid robotics offer greater opportunities for South Korean suppliers, but they appear to have raised concerns about the competitive gap too. Such mixed reactions reflect the complex responses that the rise of AI-driven smart industries can provoke. Today, humanoid robotics is emerging as a new frontier in AI development. The sector will create greater demand not only for robots but also for high-end chips, sensors and other electronic components the robots could rely on. Competition between China and South Korea seems to be inevitable, but it is only one part of a bigger picture. Humanoid robotics depends on a broad network of suppliers, creating opportunities for companies in the two countries to share at different stages of the supply chain. As China's industry expands, South Korean suppliers could find greater markets for their components. And, China and South Korea bring different strengths to the evolution of humanoid robotics. China's capabilities in robot manufacturing, supply-chain scale and real-world application scenarios provide a foundation for the industry's expansion. South Korea has accumulated expertise in semiconductors and electronic components used in these robots. The industry's growth could create more chances for greater complementarity, with expanding robot production potentially opening up additional markets for South Korean suppliers. The humanoid robotics sector is just one example. The same logic applies to the broader AI industry, where advances are creating new products, new applications and new markets. Therefore, China's technological progress need not be viewed by South Korea solely as a competitive challenge. Instead, it could open up new windows for broader bilateral cooperation. The greater potential for complementarity in high-end manufacturing is reflected in recent trade data. In September, South Korea's exports to China rose 122.7 percent to reach $26.01 billion, exceeding $20 billion for a fourth consecutive month. Semiconductors, wireless communication components and computers were among the main drivers of that growth. These figures point to growing demand in China for South Korean products, suggesting that the expansion of China's AI-related industries is creating greater opportunities for South Korean component manufacturers. As AI drives a new wave of high-end industrial development, South Korea's opportunity may lie not in viewing China's technological progress as a competitive challenge, but in finding ways to expand bilateral cooperation and share the greater benefits of cooperation.
